output.summary: The September 15-16, 2026 minutes read decidedly hawkish. On inflation, several participants saw core services-ex-housing and core goods inflation still elevated, some saw underlying inflation above 2 percent and moving sideways, and inflation risks were widely judged skewed to the upside (energy, AI demand, possible further tariffs), with some fearing de-anchoring after more than five years above target; one dovish offset is a few participants citing a material decline in 3-month core PCE (though cautioned as volatile). On the labour market, a majority judged it had strengthened a bit with job gains outpacing labor force growth and it near maximum employment, though several noted unusually low dynamism and some said wage growth was moderate and not an inflation source. On policy, all supported the 1/4-point hike to 3-3/4 to 4 percent; many framed a higher path as prudent insurance, a number saw it necessary on their modal outlooks, several viewed the rate as not or only mildly restrictive, and most expected another increase by year end—while stressing data dependence. Net lean is hawkish (+6), tempered by the open-minded, data-dependent framing and the few dovish inflation/wage observations.

output.summary: The September minutes are decisively hawkish. Participants judged inflation elevated with insufficient progress; several cited elevated core services and core goods inflation, some saw underlying inflation above target, many reported increased business cost pressures, and inflation risks were seen as skewed to the upside (with some saying more so recently). The labour market was viewed as near maximum employment with a majority seeing recent strengthening, though some noted moderate aggregate wage growth. On policy, all participants backed the September hike, several viewed the rate as not restrictive or only mildly so, and most expected another increase would likely be appropriate by year end—while stressing data-dependence and an open mind. The only clearly dovish notes were observations that aggregate wages were moderate and that BEA methodology changes would trim some PCE contributions. With the next decision on 2026-10-28, the balance tilts hawkish (+6). Mitigating factors limit a maximal reading.

output.summary: The minutes lean hawkish. On inflation, 'several' participants flagged elevated core services ex-housing and core goods inflation, 'some' judged underlying inflation above 2% and moving sideways, and 'several' noted elevated short-term inflation expectations; only 'a few' (BEA methodology) and 'some' (moderate wage growth) offered dovish qualifications. On the labor market, a majority saw it strengthen a bit and generally near maximum employment, with risks broadly balanced. On the policy path, 'most' participants expected another rate increase would likely be appropriate by year end, 'many' called a higher path prudent on risk-management grounds, 'a number' viewed it necessary on their modal outlook, and 'several' saw current policy as not restrictive or only mildly restrictive. On risks, inflation risks were generally skewed to the upside (energy, AI demand, tariffs, expectations). What would change their minds: they stressed an 'open mind' and data-dependence at future meetings. Net lean hawkish for the next decision; +6 bp tilt. Watch-outs list was 'none'.

output.summary: The September 15-16, 2026 minutes lean clearly hawkish. On inflation, participants said it \"remained elevated and that they had not seen sufficient progress,\" with several flagging elevated core services and core goods, some seeing underlying inflation above 2 percent, and several noting elevated short-term inflation expectations; only a few cited the softer 3-month core PCE measure (while cautioning it understates inflation). On the labor market, a majority judged it had \"strengthened a bit recently\" and risks were \"broadly balanced,\" with some seeing strong AI-related wage gains, though some countered that aggregate wage growth was moderate and not an inflation source. On risks, participants \"generally assessed inflation risk as skewed to the upside,\" citing energy prices, the AI buildout, and possible further tariffs. On policy, many saw a higher path as prudent risk-management insurance, a number saw it as necessary on their modal outlooks, several saw the rate as not or only mildly restrictive, and most expected another increase would likely be appropriate by year end. The main dovish/neutral offsets were low labor-market dynamism, moderate aggregate wage growth, balanced labor risks, and the data-dependent \"open mind\" caveat. Watch-outs: none specified. Net implication for the next (Oct 27-28) decision is modestly hawkish.

output.summary: The September 2026 minutes are strongly hawkish. Participants said inflation remained elevated with insufficient progress; several flagged elevated core services ex-housing and core goods inflation, some judged underlying inflation above 2 percent, and several noted elevated short-term inflation expectations. Many cited business reports of rising cost pressures and inflation risks skewed to the upside (energy, AI buildout, tariffs). On the labor market, a majority saw it strengthening a bit and near maximum employment, though some noted it was not a source of inflation pressure. On policy, all supported the September hike; many saw a higher path as prudent insurance, a number viewed it as necessary on their modal outlooks, several judged current policy not restrictive or only mildly so, and most expected another increase by year end. The main offsetting (dovish) notes were that software/portfolio-fee effects would shrink with BEA changes and that aggregate wage growth was moderate. Minds would change based on incoming information and the balance of risks. Net lean points hawkish for the next decision.
